items.title: Inference engine in game scripting language using macros
items.story_key: story|title:inference engine in game scripting language using macros
items.content_excerpt: daslang started in 2019 at Gaijin Entertainment. Back then we called it daScript. The brief was narrow: a scripting language fast enough for game logic over an entity-component system, so that nothing ever has to be rewritten in C++ later. Strong static typing, a fast compiler, no data marshaling whatsoever. Three ways to run the same source: an interpreter for iteration or live patching, ahead-of-time C++ for shipping, and an LLVM-based JIT. It did the job. It has been running in production at Gaijin ever since. We never stopped making it faster. We recently wrote an engine for LLMs, speech recognition (ASR) and text-to-speech (TTS) in it, called dasllama. No C++, no shaders written separately in HLSL, MSL, GLSL or CUDA. All daslang. Benchmarks took an unexpected amount of effort. But now we can actually say that dasllama has its moments: Source: the ladder , dasllama 0.6.6, measured 2026-10-21/22; the two RTX 5060 Ti rows 2026-10-25, the bench built at 896bd646d. We also lose some rows, and they are on the same page. In 2026 a game team wanted a voice translator. You are in a random squad. Your squadmate just cursed at you in a language you do not know. Now the game should transcribe, translate and speak it back. Live. Loud. Here is the kicker: the GPU is busy, and not with tokens (shocking). It's drawing. So the translator has to run next to the game on whatever scraps are left of the CPU the player owns. llama.cpp was the obvious choice until it was not. It did not hit the latency mark. It's a very large dependency that's hard to integrate; all that for the sake of a few small models. Let's try daslang. After all, the language was fast enough for games. What could possibly go wrong? The first port was Whisper, on an M1. It came out about 5x faster than whisper.cpp of the day. whisper.cpp has done some excellent work since; we did not sleep much either. As we added more models, the trend continued. It still holds today: The first kernel was written by hand, and it's no longer with us. Because the second one made the scope obvious: every operation times every weight format times every CPU times every model shape. That's something you do when you have a hundred contributors each tuning their own box. So instead of writing the third kernel, we wrote a macro. daslang has Lisp/Haxe-style macros: compile-time code that reads and rewrites the AST. They made dasllama possible and sometimes even interesting. [tune] was the first thing which came online. Just aft

items.title: The LLM Engineer's Schedule
items.content_excerpt: The Maker’s and Manager’s Schedule are famous idiom’s for how individual contributors and managers contribute successfully to a business. The former needs long uninterrupted timeblocks, to focus on an individual task. Whereas the later, managers, can quickly hop from task to task (meeting to meeting). These two schedules heavily conflicted with each other. Interrupting a maker in the middle of their timeblock costs more than just that interruption, it also costs the time to ramp down and ramp back up, a singular meeting within a focus time block could easily nullify its effectiveness . Not allowing Manager’s to schedule meetings inhibits them from doing their job. LLM’s have put a twist into this equation. Makers now have tireless, perpetually working machines. Giving makers constant uninterrupted background timeblocks with the ability to engage in meetings. Each company has it’s own cultures and expectations of how long an engineer would work but there was an inevitability that developers would eventually sleep and productivity would halt. The LLM engineer themselves will not always be working, but those that do not have agents running 24/7 will be left behind. Engineers will need to build the skills, processes and orchestration that enables them to kick off an agent and let it run autonomously for 12+ hours and come back to meaningful results the next day. Working on the right thing is certainly more important than working on the wrong thing , but so is doing that faster and iterating quickly to figure out what the right thing is . Both of these are facilitated by properly allocating your time. The morning, similar to the past, is reserved for deep work. Kicking off new strands of work and iterating on past agent runs. New agent runs will require building context (for the engineer and the agent), understanding the problem space, available solutions, trade-offs , testing, deploying and monitoring strategies. Once those have been established a well defined prompt, with clear outcomes and next steps, can be crafted and sent off on its way. It’s imperative that the agent has a success criteria to iterate on themselves and for this to serve as your basis for judging its work later. The agent will inevitably make some mistake, small ones can be absorbed or ignored, catastrophic mistakes that invalidate the agents work waste your time. items.title: Show HN: Hey Spark – open-source voice assistant for your laptop, any LLM brain
items.story_key: story|title:hey spark open source voice assistant for your laptop any llm brain
items.content_excerpt: Hey Spark, by ContextuAI: a wake-word voice assistant with Claude, Hermes Agent or any OpenAI-compatible model as the brain and MCP servers as connectors An always-listening voice assistant for your laptop. Say "Hey Spark" , ask a question or give a command, and hear the answer. The wake word, speech recognition and voice all run locally on your CPU. The brain is Claude, Hermes Agent , or any OpenAI-compatible model, including a local one through Ollama. Spark reaches your tools (GitHub, Gmail, Calendar, your own systems) through MCP servers, and it asks out loud before doing anything that changes something. "Hey Spark, what's on my calendar tomorrow?" "Set a pasta timer for ten minutes." "Summarize the open pull requests on hey-spark." "Let's start a new project called weather-bot." → "I'll create a folder, a git repo and a private GitHub repo called weather-bot. Should I go ahead?" Nothing leaves your machine before the wake word. After it, only the text of your request goes to the brain you chose. Audio leaves the machine only if you pick a cloud STT backend. Requirements: macOS 14 or later on Apple Silicon, or Windows 11 (see Platform support ), a microphone, about 1 GB of disk for models, and a brain: Claude Code signed in to your Claude account (or with an Anthropic API key ), an OpenAI-compatible key, or Ollama running locally. A USB speakerphone with echo cancellation works best. Get the latest build from Releases . Each file has a .sha256 checksum next to it. Settings, logs, models and your .env live in ~/Library/Application Support/HeySpark . No microphone handy? uv run spark --text lets you type questions and read answers, and uv run spark --brain mock --text runs fully offline with no key at all. The easiest way to switch is the desktop app's Brain window, which also tests the connection and checks that the model can call tools. See docs/openai_brain.md for the provider presets and the config.yaml settings. With Claude, brain.mode picks the models: auto (default) sends quick requests to brain.fast_model and bigger ones to brain.deep_model ; deep answers everything with brain.deep_model and hands tool-heavy lookups to a researcher on a faster model (the best answers, and the highest API cost). You can also switch by voice ("use the deep model", "back to auto"). The default config.yaml uses the bundled model assets/wakewords/hey_spark.onnx . Nothing to set up. If it misses you or wakes on its own, tune wakeword.options.openwakeword.threshold . Wa

items.title: Agents Prompt People: Using Agents for Long-Horizon Financial Work
items.summary: Arca's head of AI discusses persistent memory, the benefits of a custom harness, and agentic workflows that span days.
items.story_key: story|title:agents prompt people using agents for long horizon financial work
items.content_excerpt: Keyword matches words; semantic matches meaning and exact titles or names; hybrid combines both. In keyword mode, use quotation marks for exact phrases. Author matches published credits. Year applies to posts; wiki entries have no author or publication year. You can also use author:"Ada" or type:podcast in non-regex searches. Arca's head of AI discusses persistent memory, the benefits of a custom harness, and agentic workflows that span days. At AI Engineer New York this month, we sat down with Aman Singh , the lead AI Engineer at Arca , an “AI-native” company providing wealth management services. We discovered that while agents do most of the background work in the firm, there are guardrails in place to ensure that human advisors are making the final decisions. The goal is for AI to guide the process; or as Singh nicely put it, “agents prompt people more than people prompt agents.” Arca recently raised $48.5 Million in a round led by General Catalyst, with participation from Index Ventures and Venrock. One of the features of using AI in financial services, explained Singh, is that it’s typically long-horizon work — although not long-running. In his AIE presentation, Singh noted that agent tasks at Arca can take up to ten days. “It's very stop-start, there's many actors in between, many decision points, many handoffs,” he said. “So we have this persistence for every client ,” Singh said in our podcast discussion. “What has happened so far? What are we tracking for next? What needs to happen immediately in the next couple of days [and] what are we tracking for the long term? Which individual is responsible for which action? All of this is being tracked by our memory systems that our agents contribute to.” Arca uses models from frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, with Claude its primary model provider. The company has built its own harness , which automatically selects the best model to use for a particular task, based on the company’s internal benchmarks. Owning the harness, rather than using a managed agent harness, also means that Arca has the flexibility to change model providers if it needs to. Safety is obviously key for financial services. Singh noted that although agents do much of the work, an agent’s role is limited to analysis and proposing solutions. Trading and any other money movement is handled by a human advisor. “All of our safety restrictions are fully deterministic,” he said. “And they take the decision making off the agent's hands.”

items.title: What’s new in AI infrastructure and orchestration in October
items.summary:
The Google Cloud AI Infrastructure team had another busy month in October, filled with new product launches and updates to power today’s AI and agentic workloads scalably and efficiently. We were also honored to share our progress with customers, partners, and the broader community at leading industry events, including NVIDIA GTC, PyTorch Conference, and AGNTCon + MCPCon. Let’s dive in!

Product, technology, and tools updates

  • New compute service: Agent Compute Engine is a purpose-built compute service providing high-performance, hardware-isolated microVM sandboxes alongside expanded agent governance capabilities like Agent Gateway and Agent Registry, all in the service of securing and scaling autonomous AI agents. Its primary benefits include rapid sub-second activation, extreme workload density through copy-on-write memory sharing, enterprise-grade security and identity management, and cross-cloud observability.

  • AI Hypercomputer updates: At NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026 we announced updates to our agentic infrastructure, including to A5X instances powered by the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 platform, Virgo Network scale-out fabric, and Managed Lustre storage. These co-engineered advancements provide enterprises with accelerated performance, enhanced sovereign AI controls, while advanced Confidential Computing capabilities help you train and deploy complex multi-step models securely and efficiently.

  • GKE product update: CPU startup boost for GKE, in preview, uses Kubernetes In-place Pod Resize to dynamically elevate container CPU resources during initialization and scale them back down to steady-state levels without having to restart the containers. This feature removes startup throttling and accelerates cold starts by up to 2x for demanding workloads, helping to lower cloud infrastructure costs.

  • GKE product update: The preview of the Wiz Runtime Sensor add-on for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) brings low-touch deployment, automated lifecycle management, enterprise credential security, and fleet-wide governance to Wiz's eBPF runtime threat detection for both Standard and Autopilot GKE clusters.

  • Modernization tools: Together at last. Google Cloud Modernize brings Google Cloud’s migration and modernization tools, including Migration Center, Google Cloud VMware Engine, Google Cloud Mainframe Modernization and our new EKS-to-GKE Migration Agent, into a single portfolio. Enterprise teams now have purpose-built agentic capabilities across infrastructure assessment, platform modernization, and application modernization.

  • Cloud Run product update: Temporal Serverless Workers on Cloud Run automatically scale worker pools based on Temporal task queue demands and scale down to zero when idle. This integration eliminates cluster management, lowers costs, using Temporal Worker Versioning to safely handle stateful, long-running workflows and AI agent workloads.

  • New open-source product: llm-d 1.0 is an open-source, Kubernetes-native serving stack that turns a cluster of model servers into a coordinated serving pool, unifying distributed LLM inference across mixed Google Cloud TPU and GPU fleets. Co-founded by Google and partners, it provides production-ready benefits such as cache-aware routing, tiered KV cache offloading, and priority-based flow control to dramatically improve context reuse, reduce time-to-first-token latency, and efficiently scale multi-tenant agent workloads.

  • New open-source product: Working with Meta, we open-sourced TorchTPU, a native PyTorch stack that integrates Google TPUs directly into the PyTorch ecosystem alongside GPUs and CPUs. Now developers can train, serve, and deploy models natively on TPUs using familiar frameworks like Hugging Face, vLLM, and TorchTitan.

  • Google Distributed Cloud updates: Organizations that operate under strict sovereignty mandates would love to use AI to help them process data, but can’t send it to the cloud. The latest version of Google Distributed Cloud (GDC) air-gapped brings frontier AI models and multimodal enterprise search with Gemini into these isolated environments. In addition, GDC air-gapped supports NVIDIA HGX B300 systems based on the NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra architecture, and features enhanced networking and security capabilities. 

  • Edge inference product: Google open-sourced ML Drift, a cross-platform on-device GPU compute engine built for LiteRT that abstracts hardware complexities across OpenGL ES, OpenCL, Metal, and WebGPU. The framework delivers peak performance, enhanced 5D tensor support, and memory efficiency for both classical machine learning workloads and advanced generative AI models at the edge.

  • Open-weight model support: Reflection's Beam is an open-weight, 501-parameter model released under an Apache 2.0 license designed specifically for frontier software engineering and long-horizon agentic tasks. We announced day 0 support and ready-to-run deployment recipes for service Beam on AI Hypercomputer and NVIDIA AI Infrastructure.

Practitioner guides and how-tos

  • AI network reference architectures: In Networking for AI inference model serving - GKE only and for all other backends, learn about reference architectures for AI inference model serving that provide centralized governance and private IP routing using Private Service Connect, Apigee API Management, and Model Armor. These architectures simplify multi-model scaling and prompt security across GKE, Cloud Run, and hybrid clouds. 

  • How-to guide: A Tale of TPU Observability on GKE: Part 2 - Dynamic Slicing Enhancements breaks down GKE's new Dynamic Slicing observability tools and metrics for next-generation v7 TPUs through an engaging, story-driven observability guide featuring Alex, a lead AI platform engineer. Explore the step-by-step diagnostic workflows with real-world examples and handy command-line snippets. Check out Part 1 here.

Customer and partner updates

  • AI21 achieves an 83% reduction in time-to-start for AI workloads with AI Hypercomputer: Frontier lab AI21 needed a new stack on which to train its Jamba family, and chose AI Hypercomputer configured with GKE on A3 and A3 Ultra instances. By doing so, AI21 says it cut high-priority job wait times from 72 hours to 12, and manual scheduling interventions from 20 per week to zero.

  • Visko streams real-time world models on Google Cloud TPUs: Visko, an AI startup developing interactive world models, deployed an end-to-end live inference pipeline that combines video generation, super-resolution upscaling, and synchronized audio onto a single Cloud TPU slice. In this blog, the team discusses how it engineered the pipeline, the architectural optimizations it made, and practical lessons for other startups building ultra-low-latency generative AI.

  • ZenteiQ scales physical AI inference 4x with GKE and llm-d: In order to pre-train models that understand physical laws, governing equations, and numerical solvers, Indian AI startup ZenteiQ designed and built a large-scale batch synthetic data-generation pipeline that runs across multiple model families and feeds verified datasets into training runs. GKE and GKE Inference Gateway gave ZenteiQ the inference-routing layer within its pipeline to scale aggregate inference throughput 4.07x and grow daily output from 1.47 billion to 5.97 billion generated tokens for every 1,000 accelerators.

  • Palo Alto Networks modernizes cloud-delivered security service: Palo Alto has worked with Google Cloud since 2018 to deliver its Prisma Access security service, and it was time to update it. In order not to compromise its security guarantees, Palo Alto separated the platform into two independently scalable layers: an ingress layer that handles traffic routing and forwarding running on GKE, with Axion C4A instances; and a security layer that handles threat inspection, running on dedicated single-tenant VMs fronted by an Internal Load Balancer. Each layer can now scale, update, and operate independently. 

  • Oracle is the first hyperscaler to provide TPUs outside Google Cloud: By deploying Google TPUs, Oracle is broadening the range of AI chips available through its Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), and giving customers more options for running AI workloads. Google TPUs on OCI will be available in 2027.

Research, reports and deep-dives

  • New resource: As enterprise organizations shift from isolated AI experiments to production-scale systems, different departments — from engineering and finance to executive leadership — often speak different technical dialects; The Encyclopedia of AI Infrastructure bridges that communication gap by demystifying complex infrastructure jargon.

  • Analyst report: We are thrilled to announce that Google was named a Leader in the inaugural 2026 IDC MarketScape for Agentic AI Platforms. 

  • Deep dive: A companion technical guide describing the architecture of Agent Compute Engine and how Google’s Gemini team needed both the isolation of a VM and the speed and density of a container to deliver personal agents for every Gemini user.

September 2026

Product, technology, and tools updates

Google Kubernetes Engine updates: The GKE team is all about improving the scalability of the platform, and in September, those improvements came in many shapes and sizes:

  • New feature: Need an execution runtime with higher density for your agentic workloads? We engineered the new open-source GKE Agent Substrate to run millions of sandboxes with 10x higher density than standard container runtimes. Agent Substrate also delivers sub-500ms resume operations at over 500 suspend/resume activations per second with a native zero-trust kernel and network isolation. 

  • Product update: GKE now has scale-to-zero capabilities built-in. No need to configure complex components to scale your workloads down, thanks to the HPA with the Autoscaling Metric and support for KEP-2021, which do the job for you, out of the box. Read the blog to learn more. 

  • Product update: Further, the GKE HPA (with the above-mentioned Autoscaling Metric) now lets you scale up and down based on custom PromQL metrics, in addition to standard metrics, allowing you to trigger workloads according to conditions that are meaningful and unique to your business. Read more here. 

  • New feature: Yet another scalability feature is GKE Pod snapshots, which lets you save the running state of your workload, including CPU and GPU memory, and restore it on demand. According to internal tests, GKE Pod snapshots can reduce AI inference start-up by as much as 89%. Learn more here.

  • New migration tool: Finally, if you’ve always wanted to migrate your container workloads from AWS EKS to GKE but feared a daunting, high-friction engineering endeavor, we’ve just launched GKE agentic migration, a purpose-built agent plugin that replaces brittle, ad-hoc prompting with an AI-assisted migration pipeline protected by deterministic guardrails. Designed as a compilation of agent skills and a local Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, it uses AI to translate complex AWS EKS IaC and Kubernetes manifests directly into GKE landing zones. Get started with the onboarding guide.

  • Feature updates: Reinforcement learning (RL) and evaluation workloads are a beast: In a standard agentic RL loop, an LLM policy generates actions like code snippets on GPUs and executes them inside isolated CPU sandboxes to observe a reward signal. However, when scaling up this loop to support tens of thousands of parallel rollouts, infrastructure bottlenecks emerge, for instance idle accelerators, image cardinality, and a saturated control plane. To help, we developed GKE Agent Sandbox optimized for RL, plus an Agent Sandbox RL orchestration SDK and native integrations for popular RL gyms and harnesses. All are now generally available, and you can learn more here.

Storage updates: AI trains and creates lots of data, and that data has to live somewhere — in block storage systems, file systems, object stores and databases. We announced enhancements to our storage portfolio to help this critical layer roll with the agentic punches:  

  • Product update: Filestore agent volumes offer high-performance, elastic, persistent file storage for agentic workloads. Thanks to its tight integration with GKE Agent Substrate and GKE Agent Sandbox, Filestore agent volumes automatically allocates and attaches a dedicated, isolated file workspace to GKE agent sandboxes in milliseconds. Request access to the preview here. 

  • New product: If you run generative AI and RAG data layers  — think Milvus, Pinecone, Qdrant, Vespa, Redis, and in-memory context caching — you may want to take a look at the M4N family of VMs, now GA, which offers the highest per-core IOPS and throughput of leading hyperscalers. Paired with Google Cloud's custom Titanium offload architecture and paired with Hyperdisk Extreme, M4N instances deliver up to 25,000 MiB/s (25 GiB/s) of aggregate host storage performance and up to 1 million IOPS. 

  • New product: Another new Compute Engine product, Z4D, is GA, and a strong storage solution for AI/ML training and inference workloads. When configured as a bare metal instance, Z4D provides both the high local SSD (LSSD) capacity and low latency required by agentic microVMs, so you can run thousands of isolated sandboxes per host with native performance and efficiency. Learn about Z4D machines here.

  • Product update: Today’s AI training and inference pipelines create data faster than most storage management systems can keep up, creating challenges for teams trying to understand their storage estates. A new version of Storage Intelligence advisor makes it easier to answer the question: "What’s in my buckets?" and quickly identify unexpected changes. Then, enhanced batch operations let you automate bulk changes across your buckets — say, move storage classes, mass-delete stale or temporary data, or apply metadata, tagging, retention, or encryption changes. Learn about the latest in Storage Intelligence advisor here.

  • New product: Last but not least, a new version of AlloyDB for PostgreSQL brings together pioneering Google infrastructure — Colossus distributed file system, and Jupiter network — to power a new, no-compromises database architecture for the agentic era. 

Practitioner guides and how-tos

  • How-to: Wish you could make GPUs and TPUs scattered around the globe behave as a single pool behind a single entry point? In this blog, we show you how to do just that. At the edge, the multi-cluster GKE Inference Gateway focuses on global, multi-region traffic distribution and high availability. Beneath that, the LLM-d router handles complex, memory-aware scheduling algorithms to keep utilization high. This architecture is deliberately runtime-, model-, and accelerator-agnostic, and in tests, routing traffic through the multi-cluster GKE Inference Gateway added less than 1% overhead.

  • Guide: Using or planning to use GKE on TPUs for AI model training or inference? Training massive Large Language Models (LLMs) or running high-throughput inference serving represents a significant investment in specialized AI hardware, such as Cloud TPUs and GPUs. To get the most out of every dollar spent, you need to understand workload lifecycle metrics in GKE. This detailed guide explains how to turn opaque cluster behaviors into actionable telemetry.

Customer and partner updates

  • GKE customer: Learn why gaming startup SeaVerse relies on GKE Agent Sandbox for its multi-tenant workloads, and how the platform helped it decrease its infrastructure costs by 60%. 

Research, reports and deep-dives

In case you missed it, we’re also thrilled to share that Google has been named a leader, including achieving the highest score on either product or strategy, in three key analyst reports from Gartner and Forrester. 

  • Google is a leader in The Forrester Wave™: Public Cloud Platforms, Q3 2026: Highest overall score of any cloud provider!
  • Google named a Leader in 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Strategic Cloud Platform Services: Positioned furthest for “Completeness of Vision” of all vendors evaluated.
  • Google is a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Container Management: Positioned highest in “Ability to Execute” of all vendors evaluated.
  • Google Cloud achieved a Gold rating in the latest SemiAnalysis ClusterMax 3.0 report, which evaluates the reliability, performance, support, pricing, and security of GPU providers globally. See the full report for more.

August 2026

Product, technology, and tools updates

  • Product update: Filestore, Google Cloud’s first-party, secure, scalable NFS file service, has emerged as a popular storage platform for AI and agentic workflows, and now, it’s even better suited to the task, with a new backend storage layer built directly on Colossus, Google’s foundational distributed storage system. This new backend lets you provision IOPS independently from storage capacity, and is deeply integrated with GKE. In AI environments, this can help you service so-called agentic swarms — large groups of agents that need to read and write to a common dataset — without a drop off in performance. For more, check out the blog post. 

  • New feature: gVisor sandboxes are now available in distributed Ray clusters on GKE. In partnership with Anyscale, we introduced an experimental library for Ray that brings gVisor, Google’s open-source application kernel, directly into distributed Ray clusters. gVisor provides lightweight environments with stronger isolation than ordinary containers, plus fast startup times and low memory overhead. To try out these sandboxing capabilities on GKE, head over to the Ray sandboxing User Guide.

  • Product update: Looking for high-performance, easy-to-use infrastructure on which to run a personal AI agent, but don’t want to spend a lot of money? New Cloud Run instances are dedicated, singleton compute runtimes on Cloud Run that won’t shut down when the agent is idle. Better yet, the cost to run a Cloud Run instance with 1 vCPU and 1 GiB of memory continuously for 30 days is just $5.70.  

Practitioner guides, documentation and how-tos

  • How-to guide: Big news in Model Context Protocol (MCP) land: As of the 2026-07-28 specification, the protocol core is “completely stateless. The handshake is gone. The initialize / initialized handshake (SEP-2575) and the logical Mcp-Session-Id header (SEP-2567) have been removed entirely. Instead, every request is now self-describing and independent.” Whoa. Learn more about the changes that the latest MCP specification brings, and more importantly, how to implement them, in this Google Developers blog.  
  • Guide: Real-time AI systems make a mess of traditional network load balancing techniques. “Instead of handling isolated requests, the backend has to manage a continuous, live bidirectional stream. You’re dealing with a constant stream of audio chunks, transcripts, model outputs, and synthesized speech flowing back and forth simultaneously.” Things only get worse when the user gets involved. “The server has to immediately halt its current speech generation, pivot to update the context, maybe trigger a new tool, and start drafting a different response; this must be done without dropping the connection.” For a new approach to managing load in the AI era, read Scaling real-time AI agents with session-aware load balancing.
  • How-to: Learn how to build an elastic, scalable LLM inference platform on GKE, even with a mix of different GPU accelerators. The proposed architecture combines Capacity Advisor and Compute Advisor, plus high-performance storage like RunAI:model streamer or GCPFuse with parallel downloads. Get all the details here.
  • Documentation: The thing about hosts with GPUs or TPUs is that you can’t use live migration to update them, setting up a maintenance challenge. In this new docs page, learn how to update accelerator-equipped hosts according to your tolerance for downtime for your training and inference workloads.    
  • Documentation: Advanced Compute Images, or ACIs, are standardized image stacks for AI/ML and HPC infrastructure, so you don’t need to manually build your own custom images. In this new docs page, learn how to create an ACI image using the Google Cloud CLI, console, or SchedMD's Slurm workload manager. 
  • Guide: AI workloads are notoriously difficult to architect, resource-intensive, and bursty, which can also lead to scaling bottlenecks and large pools of underutilized — or misutilized — compute resources. A new blog outlines the three main ways to achieve dynamic capacity management in Google Cloud: 1) scheduling capacity for planned downtime; 2) maintaining automated fallback capacity for unplanned downtime; and 3) relying on GKE’s core orchestration capabilities to automate resource allocation. 

Customer and partner updates

  • Business orchestration software provider UiPath was dealing with spiky workloads, and wanted more predictable costs. To get there, it re-architected its infrastructure, moving from isolated clusters to a shared Google Cloud GPU fleet that included both A3 VM instances (NVIDIA H100 GPUs) for training with G4 VM instances (NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs) for inference. You can read more about their architecture here. 

  • Mirendil, an frontier AI lab focused on accelerating AI development, announced that it is using AI Hypercomputer with both TPUs and NVIDIA GPUs to support its model pre-training and post-training applications. 

  • Replenit, a retail CRM provider, built its AI decision engine in Google Cloud, using BigQuery, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and open-source Gemma models that it runs on Cloud TPUs. This latter combination provided Replenit with 90% lower pipeline costs than their previous cloud provider, the company reports. Read the full case study for more. 

  • Malachyte architected its AI-powered e-commerce recommendation platform on top of Bigtable, Managed Service for Apache Kafka, Pub/Sub, Compute Engine, and last but not least, GKE. See how it all comes together in this blog.

July 2026

Product, technology, and tools updates

  • Product update: Google Cloud Managed Lustre is now GA, and available in four distinct performance tiers that deliver throughput ranging from 125 MB/s, 250 MB/s, 500 MB/s, to 1000 MB/s per TiB of capacity — with the ability to scale up to 8 PB of storage capacity. The Managed Lustre solution is powered by DDN’s EXAScaler, combining DDN's decades of leadership in high-performance storage with Google Cloud's expertise in cloud infrastructure.

  • Product update: C4N network and storage optimized VMs are now GA. C4N is our first network- and block-storage-optimized VM series built to eliminate data-transfer bottlenecks. Powered by 5th Gen Intel Xeon Scalable processors and built on Google's Titanium offloading hardware, it achieves 400 Gbps network bandwidth, 95 million packets per second (MPPS), and up to 25 GiB/s of block storage throughput when paired with Hyperdisk Extreme.

  • New feature: GKE Dataplane V2 up to 15K Nodes with Network Policies (GA). This capability enables standard GKE clusters to scale up to 15,000 nodes while maintaining full active Network Policy enforcement, supporting the massive infrastructure needs of large enterprise and AI/ML customers.

  • New feature: Co-operative time-slicing in llm-d. If you’re running reinforcement learning (RL) workloads, you can now interleave independent RL jobs onto shared physical hardware, increasing aggregate accelerator duty cycles from a ~40% baseline up to 70% without impacting model convergence or accuracy. 

  • New AI security tool: Looking to secure your AI supply chain on GKE, deploy AI workloads safely, and cut down on shadow AI? We open-sourced k8s-aibom, a lightweight, unprivileged Kubernetes controller that continuously monitors container clusters to automatically detect running AI runtimes (like vLLM and Triton) and generate standard CycloneDX Machine Learning Bill of Materials (ML-BOMs). Check out the k8s-aibom project and get involved.

Practitioner guides and how-tos

  • How-to guide: On July 27, Google announced Day 0 support for Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight model, the day weights were released. Whichever your preferred deployment path — via Model Garden, custom orchestration, or GKE with llm-d recipes — this guide offers detailed step-by-step instructions to help you evaluate and pilot Kimi K3 in Google Cloud. 

  • How-to guide: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) managed DRANET supports both GPUs and TPUs. There are several configurations to use this implementation, including standard cluster (where you have full control) and autopilot cluster (where Google does the heavy configs for you). Take a deeper dive in the hands-on lab, GKE Autopilot clusters with TPUs, GKE managed DRANET and Gemma 4.

  • How-to guide: Learn to run Ray on TPUs, not GPUs. In Part 1 of this two-part series, we discuss TPU slices (hint: Ray thinks of them as just another accelerator on which to schedule), then walk through Ray’s various AI libraries (Part 2).

  • How-to guide: Evaluate TPUs for sample workloads using a new microbenchmark suite that helps you accurately assess whether a device is achieving its theoretical performance specifications, and to identify specific performance gaps or architecture-specific bottlenecks. Dive in here. 

  • How-to guide: Scale your agents without killing your budget. Learn how GKE orchestration can help you safely pack more agents onto a fixed compute footprint with GKE Agent Sandbox and Pod snapshots. Whether your goal is performance or cost optimization, we teach you how to turn the right dials for optimal agent efficiency. 

  • Technical blueprint: Inside the optimization of Mistral 3 large inference on Ironwood. This blog outlines how one Google team optimized Mistral 3 large MoE model inference on Google’s Ironwood (TPU v7x), achieving a 1.5x performance gain. They did so with hybrid sharding, replacing linear VPU summations with tree reductions, optimizing GMM/MLA kernels, and adopting asynchronous scheduling. As a result, they boosted throughput by up to 48% while maintaining benchmark accuracy neutrality. Read the full blog here.

Research, reports and deep-dives

  • Report: Google was named a Leader in the inaugural GartnerⓇ Magic Quadrant™ for AI Infrastructure, positioned highest for ‘Ability to Execute’ and furthest for ‘Completeness of Vision’. Gartner called out Google’s proprietary scalable compute, integrated AI Hypercomputer architecture, and the scale of our AI compute capacity as key strengths. Download a copy here.

  • Report: We recently surveyed more than 1,400 senior IT leaders for our State of AI Infrastructure report, and a resounding pattern emerged: The gap between AI ambition and infrastructure reality is widening. In fact, 83% of organizations say they require infrastructure upgrades to support production-grade agentic AI. Read the accompanying blog to understand how adapting your infrastructure to meet the demands that agentic applications place on your systems will help you move from pilot to production.

June 2026

Product, technology and tool updates

  • Product update: Protecting sensitive data used with AI is a critical part of advanced and secure cloud infrastructure. Confidential Computing cryptographically protects data in use in hardware-based Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) with verifiable data integrity, and is now available on the accelerator-optimized G4 machine series, featuring NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. Get started with Confidential G4 VMs and Confidential G4 GKE Nodes.

  • Developer resource: The new TPU Developer Hub is the place to go for model builders, optimizers, and developers to learn to unlock the full performance of Google Cloud TPUs. Read more in this blog. 

  • New product: Scale your AI workloads with the new OpenTelemetry-Based TPU AI Telemetry Collector Agent. For the first time, you can route high-fidelity TPU hardware telemetry to Google Cloud Monitoring, Google Managed Prometheus, or your own self-hosted Grafana stack.

Practitioner guides and how-tos

  • How-to guide: Learn how to build high availability into an AI inference workload running on GKE Inference Gateway with TPUs, Cloud Storage FUSE and Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA). This blog provides an overview, or you can get all the technical details in the hands-on codelab.

  • How-to guide: Did you know you can connect your AI agents to unstructured data in Cloud Storage via Model Context Protocol (MCP)? In this blog, learn about why would want to do that from three customer examples, then how to do it, choosing either a fully managed service, or a self-managed local server for more customization and control. 

Research, reports and deep-dives

  • Report: According to an independent benchmark report, GKE Inference Gateway outperforms the next leading managed Kubernetes service with 15.7% higher throughput, 92.8% shorter wait times, and 62.6% lower inter-token latency. This performance can be attributed to its use of prefix caching, which optimizes LLM performance by storing the KV cache (activation states) of long, repetitive prompt prefixes. Learn more in the blog. 

  • Architecture deep dive: A closer look at the cold start problem, this time for TPUs and GKE, and how the Run:ai Model Streamer can help change the dynamic. 

Customer and partner updates

  • Customer win: Leveraging GKE, BigQuery, Cloud SQL, and Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Pager Health is eliminating operational fragmentation to deliver a simplified, personalized U.S. healthcare experience that transforms lives.

  • Customer win: Trustpilot, the customer review platform, built a high-volume streaming pipeline using fine-tuned Gemma models with Dataflow and Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform running on cost-optimized A2 VMs using A100 GPUs, as well as optimized version of vLLM maintained by Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

May 2026

Product, technology and tool updates

  • Product update: GKE Agent Sandbox is now generally available.

  • New open-source project: Agent Substrate is a new open-source project aimed at continuing to push the limits of agentic infrastructure density

  • New feature: Google AI Edge Portal, a solution for testing and benchmarking on-device machine learning (ML) at scale, now supports benchmarking and debugging on-device LLMs. Read more here. 

  • Product deep dive: We went into depth about Cloud Storage Rapid, a new family of high-performance storage offerings for AI workloads. At launch, offerings include Rapid Bucket (formerly Rapid Storage), a high-performance zonal object storage offering, and Rapid Cache (formerly Anywhere Cache), which accelerates reads on-demand and colocates compute and data for workloads in existing buckets. 

Research, reports and deep dives

  • Architecture deep dive: Google Global Infrastructure VP Bikash Koley and Engineering Fellow Arjun Singh provide a high-level overview of the challenges that AI workloads pose to network infrastructure, and discuss the deep enhancements we’ve made to our data center fabrics, WAN, and global networks to better support them. 

  • Architecture deep dive: We unveiled a new cluster-level reliability model for developing frontier AI models on TPUs, ditching instance-level reliability 

Customer and partner updates

  • Customer win: Visual media provider Imgix serves more than 8 billion images and videos from AI Hypercomputer equipped with G4 VMs powered by NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs.

items.title: How AI agents shape experts’ judgment calls
items.summary: In a randomized trial, professional analysts working with an AI coding agent went with the option the agent was randomly assigned to favor 86% of the time. We look at what this means for human oversight of AI-assisted work.
items.story_key: story|title:how ai agents shape experts judgment calls
items.content_excerpt: When experts hand their work to an AI agent, the usual assumption is that they still make the decisions that matter. The agent writes the code, runs the numbers, and offers advice, but the expert decides what to measure, how to interpret ambiguous evidence, and what the next steps should be. Often there is more than one reasonable answer to these questions, and the decision will come down to the experience and values of whoever makes the call. We wanted to look at whether experts really do make those important decisions, or whether in practice they defer to their AI agents. In a study we report in a new paper , we asked 50 professional analysts to do a realistic statistical analysis with Claude Code. They all had experience in causal inference—that is, working out from data whether one thing causes another. Their task was to advise a farming cooperative on whether an advisory service it was running was effective and should be expanded. Along the way, the analysts had to make four choices between two reasonable options, such as whether to measure productivity as crop yield per hectare or as yield per unit of operating cost, and then make a final decision. To see whether they were making these calls themselves, we set up each analyst’s agent to favor one option on each decision, which the analysts weren’t told about. Which way the agents would “lean” would be decided by coin flip. The agent was told to make the best honest case for its lean, to change its mind if the evidence demanded it, and never to mislead. Across the four analytical choices, analysts went with their agent’s lean 86% of the time. If the agent’s input made no difference, we’d expect about 50%. When analysts had already expressed their own preference before the agent weighed in, they switched away from it 60% of the time if the agent disagreed, compared to 6% if it agreed. Afterward, when asked to explain their choices, 77% of analysts used the agents’ own arguments—sometimes word for word—but only 15% credited the agent as the source of those arguments. Analysts who followed the agents’ recommendations closely were about as confident in their final recommendation as the rest, and roughly as likely to call it the product of their own judgment. We don’t know how much this tells us about the real world. items.title: Evaluating DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 for loss of control and harmful manipulation risks
items.summary: As frontier language models grow increasingly capable and autonomous, independent third-party evaluations are critical for characterizing their systemic safety risks. While closed-source releases are routinely accompanied by comprehensive system cards, open-weight models receive less scrutiny regarding frontier risks. To address this gap, we present an independent safety evaluation of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017, the latest version of V4.1 Flash that departs from V4 with a new architecture, scaled-up training, and strong agentic capabilities. Drawing on the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, we evaluate the model across 34 benchmarks, including 5 in-house suites, spanning evaluation integrity, loss of control, and harmful manipulation. Conforming to the AEF-1 standard, we compare V4.1 Flash-1017 against V4.1 Flash, earlier DeepSeek V4 models, and leading closed-source systems (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Gemini 3.8 Flash). Overall, V4.1 Flash-1017 shows substantial safety improvements over the V4 generation and approaches or matches leading closed-source baselines on several dimensions, while still exhibiting notable behaviors that warrant continued attention. Building on our findings, we highlight three key observations and recommendations. First, because safety can shift and even regress across minor updates, developers should integrate safety evaluation into incremental releases. Second, as final-turn outputs and end-state checks alone cannot reliably detect loss-of-control behaviors, deployments require process-level observability across both reasoning traces and action logs. Third, because public benchmarks elicit strong evaluation awareness and face data contamination risks, developing private benchmarks is essential for trustworthy frontier evaluation.

items.title: Harness Engineering: What's Actually New (And What Isn't)
items.summary:
Harness engineering is the new name for everything around the model: tools, context, guardrails, telemetry. Carly Richmond, Senior Manager of Developer Advocacy at Elastic, shows what's genuinely new about building agents, and why most of the harness still rests on software engineering fundamentals you already know.

What we cover:
– What harness engineering is, and how it builds on prompt, context and loop engineering
– What's genuinely new: non-determinism, tool calling and models that change under your feet
– Why TDD evolves into AI agent evals, and when LLM-as-a-judge is the wrong tool
– Writing tool descriptions for agents the way you'd write an OpenAPI spec
– Telemetry, guardrails and security for an agent harness

items.title: Things That Go Beep in the Night: Agentic AI Joins the Search for Extraterrestrial Signals
items.summary: While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents […]
items.story_key: story|title:things that go beep in the night agentic ai joins the search for extraterrestria
items.content_excerpt: While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents built by aliens. Some scientists have suggested that extraterrestrial civilizations, if they exist, could be billions of years older than humanity. Such civilizations might have developed technologies far beyond humanity’s, including forms of AI. Breakthrough Listen and the SETI Institute are bringing agentic AI into the daily search for extraterrestrial intelligence. At the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California, agents can now steer the instrument, enhance and correct incoming data, and apply AI models to the incoming stream — all from a single natural language request. The NVIDIA Holoscan platform processes the massive streams of sensor data, giving agents live data to act on. The result is a faster, more adaptable search for potential signals from extraterrestrial life and technologies. “As our new agentic observatories reach out into the universe, what they find may have much more in common with themselves than with the humans who created them,” said Andrew Siemion, Bernard M. Oliver chair for SETI at the SETI Institute and principal investigator of Breakthrough Listen. “But this isn’t something to fear. Rather, it’s a breakthrough in translation.” Radio telescopes generate enormous volumes of data, creating a challenge for scientists who need to identify potentially interesting signals as observations unfold. At the Allen Telescope Array, DAQIRI , a Holoscan platform library, enables the telescope to pull terabits per second of sensor data straight into GPU memory so observations are processed in flight rather than filling hard drives. CyberEther , a signal-processing framework developed at the SETI Institute, does the math using NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries including cuFFT and cuBLAS . Nexus , a web-based observatory orchestrator, acts as the agent harness. It gives agents a single source of truth for instrument state, compute resources and pipelines and lets researchers monitor packet loss, read live spectrograms and rewrite signal-processing blocks — all by prompting in natural language. items.title: claude-code v2.1.314
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added permissions.blockWritesOutsideWorkingDirectories: Write, Edit and NotebookEdit refuse paths outside the working directories in every permission mode
  • Added an optional groups list to Claude apps gateway upstreams: only developers in the listed IdP groups are sent to that upstream, on failover too
  • Added guardrail_trace to Claude apps gateway Bedrock upstreams, to log which Amazon Bedrock guardrail filter fired on a request, without the matched text
  • Added idle compaction to VS Code and Claude Desktop's Code tab: a 200K+ token conversation left idle is summarized, and the summary is used on your next message if the prompt cache has expired
  • Fixed sessions failing turn after turn with "Invalid effort level" when an organization's admin caps a model's effort: Claude Code now lowers the effort, retries, and says which level it uses
  • Fixed claude -p exiting with code 0 and no output when startup failed; it now prints the error and exits 1
  • Fixed Bedrock sessions with many images failing every turn and /compact with "400 Input is too long." instead of removing older images and compacting
  • Fixed Microsoft Foundry sessions failing when the resource has no deployment for the default Sonnet, Opus or Haiku model: Claude Code now falls back to an older model of that family
  • Fixed repeated refused requests behind a gateway that doesn't accept tool search's tool_reference blocks: the request is sent again once without tool search, and the session remembers
  • Fixed TLS connections failing with UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT when the system certificate store holds a renewed root certificate that is cross-signed with its predecessor
  • Fixed MCP servers that also work without sign-in showing "needs authentication" after their stored sign-in stopped working; they are now used signed out
  • Fixed claude mcp logout reporting success when the MCP sign-in was not removed, for example while the macOS keychain is locked over SSH
  • Fixed extra sign-in renewals when several sessions share an Anthropic profile login and the credentials lock is busy
  • Fixed claude ultrareview and claude remote-control asking the workspace trust question in a CI job that has a terminal; with CI set they now refuse an untrusted folder at once
  • Fixed an administrator's TLS trust settings in managed settings not being applied in Claude Desktop sessions
  • Fixed model switching being refused on machines with managed plugin settings when one of your own --plugin-dir or --plugin-url plugins had a broken manifest or failed to download
  • Fixed the Bedrock and Vertex model upgrade offer coming back at every start when managed settings pin the model
  • Fixed forceRemoteSettingsRefresh set only in remote managed settings no longer applying once the stored copy had expired, which let sessions start without policy when the server could not be reached
  • Fixed "Continue automatically at usage limit" continuing more than three times without a prompt from you when a task restarted itself between waits (a /goal check-in, a background or scheduled task)
  • Fixed background and cloud sessions started with Ultracode turning it back on at their next start after it had been switched off
  • Fixed the last broken reply and its retry prompts staying in the conversation after Claude gave up on a tool call that could not be parsed
  • Fixed a PreCompact hook with very large output making compaction fail or repeat; each hook's output is now cut at 10,000 characters
  • Fixed background diff refreshes briefly taking the repository's index lock, which could make a git command run at the same moment fail with "Unable to create '.git/index.lock': File exists"
  • Fixed markdown tables jumping between grid and stacked layouts on half-typed rows while streaming, and long tables falling back to raw pipes
  • Fixed the /resume picker showing the text of CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md as a session's title when the session only ran slash commands
  • Fixed /btw answering from the main conversation when asked from a subagent's open transcript
  • Fixed pasting an image over SSH to a Linux machine doing nothing silently; the prompt now says to copy the file over and paste its path
  • Fixed claude remote-control sessions that failed to start when the session service was slow for a moment: the worker's registration is now retried with growing waits
  • Fixed model switches over Remote Control that take over 8 seconds getting a "still pending" error instead of the final result
  • Fixed the sandbox.excludedCommands setting description saying listed commands always run outside the sandbox; it now says every command in a call must match an entry
  • Fixed shell and MCP calls that auto mode, a deny rule or a PreToolUse hook blocked, or that otherwise did not run, reading as if they ran in a collapsed tool group
  • Fixed sandbox protections not applying to a worktree entered by claude -p --resume or --continue
  • Fixed hooks matching Bash not running on shell commands started by the Monitor tool; such hooks can block or ask, but not approve or rewrite those commands
  • Fixed a settings file excluded with --setting-sources still supplying some settings, such as auto mode rules and saved permission consents
  • Fixed auto mode reporting a call as blocked, and listing it in /permissions, when its safety check gave no verdict
  • Fixed a Claude apps gateway Vertex upstream hanging for minutes when a Google token endpoint accepts the connection and never answers
  • Fixed the Claude apps gateway's start-up warning for a deprecated Claude Desktop key that it still serves as written saying "stops being accepted" after the key's end date
  • Fixed /upgrade opening the browser and starting a new login for plans billed through the App Store or Google Play; it now says where to change the plan
  • Fixed --resume, and rewinding past a switch to another model after a refusal, moving a session on a model name Claude Code doesn't recognize to a different model
  • Fixed requests failing when a gateway or cloud provider refuses one of Claude Code's beta headers by name: the request is sent again without it
  • Fixed model IDs spelled with a dot behind an LLM gateway, such as claude-opus-4.8, being treated as an older model with the wrong context window, output limit, effort, thinking mode and cost
  • Fixed Remote Control clients showing a stray "Compacted (ctrl+o to see full summary)" row after /compact
  • Fixed the cloud sessions tip and the Remote Control idle notice showing when an organization's policy turns those features off
  • Fixed a resumed claude.ai cloud session making a model call nobody asked for when the previous worker stopped just after receiving a new chat's files
  • Fixed WebFetch in Cowork cloud sessions silently dropping a PDF's text past 100,000 characters; it now says how much was unread and where to read on
  • Fixed Claude being told only that a command was declined after you stopped it with Esc or Stop in a cloud session or the IDE; it now also hears that the command may have run
  • Fixed blank lines at the top of a code block disappearing when the code block opens a quote
  • Fixed a blank line appearing above some ⎿ rows in the transcript view (Ctrl+O)
  • Fixed vim mode dw, dW, yw and yW carrying on past the end of the line, and made w and W stop on empty lines
  • Fixed x and Enter in the agent panel sometimes acting on the wrong agent when another agent started or finished
  • Fixed pasted text and dragged-in files being lost in Claude's question dialog unless the "Other" row had focus
  • Fixed pasted text being lost when a row in the prompt footer was selected
  • Fixed vim mode p over a character selection ignoring whether the yanked text was whole lines
  • Fixed vim mode aw and iw taking the line break at the end of a line
  • Fixed ↓ selecting footer items hidden by the ? help menu, the command list or a paste hint
  • Fixed Esc on a command's panel, such as /btw, also interrupting the subagent whose transcript is open
  • Fixed the welcome header in fullscreen mode showing the session's model while viewing a subagent or teammate that runs on a different model
  • Fixed the fullscreen transcript being left mid-conversation after "Restore conversation" in the rewind menu while scrolled up
  • Fixed a rare case where a deleted session could reappear in the resume list as an almost empty entry
  • Fixed prompts containing tags such as <bash-stdout> or <local-command-stdout> not being acknowledged to a local stream-json host
  • Fixed sessions staying untitled when the first prompt failed (for example on a usage limit) and the conversation continued afterward
  • Fixed the skill file watcher checking every removed skill kept in ~/.claude/skills/.trash, which added file system load that grew with each removal
  • Fixed the session name from /rename disappearing while Claude asks for permission or a plan decision, so side-by-side sessions stay identifiable
  • Fixed background sessions that fail to start being reported as a deleted daemon binary when the binary is still on disk
  • Fixed the tip and idle reminder about push notifications appearing when the push settings in /config are hidden or your organization has turned off Remote Control
  • Fixed ~/.claude/skills/.trash and ~/.claude/plugins/.trash growing without limit: each now holds about 1024 entries, whatever cleanupPeriodDays says
  • Fixed the Bash edit diff listing a whole file as changed when a CRLF file under git's line-ending conversion was re-saved unchanged or had one line edited
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed an idle session moving to another runner instead of pausing when the runner's request to pause it lost its connection before Anthropic answered
  • Improved memory use in long headless and SDK turns that run many subagents: the parent session no longer keeps each subagent's tool results until the turn ends
  • Improved prompt history: Ctrl+R now matches text inside collapsed [Pasted text] pills
  • Improved the /design-sync upload prompt to show the folder, the project and the files it will upload or delete
  • Improved /permissions review tab, now called Recently blocked: the footer says what Esc will do with marked rows
  • Improved auto mode's blocked calls: messages name the command, say Claude may retry and auto mode checks again, and point to /permissions to review
  • Improved permission prompts: a long reason takes fewer rows, so it pushes the command being approved off the screen on fewer terminals
  • Improved the cloud session error shown while a request refused for your claude.ai login is still being retried: it now also suggests claude auth login
  • Improved the behavior of stored claude.ai, Team, and Enterprise logins when MDM and remote settings differ on base URL or apiKeyHelper
  • Improved /config in agent view to say how to stop agent view opening by default
  • Improved session auto-titles: a session that starts with a skill or a prompt-based command such as /security-review now gets a title from it instead of staying untitled
  • Improved --resume speed and memory use on damaged transcripts
  • Improved /context speed in sessions with ten thousand or more MCP tools
  • Self-hosted runner: Improved the error shown when a session's branch isn't on the git remote: it now covers a never-pushed branch, says how to fix each case, and no longer suggests retrying
  • Updated the /claude-api skill: its Datadog setup for API tracing now sends the dd-llmobs-enabled: true header, as the Console does, and its ant install instructions drop the outdated macOS xattr step
  • Updated the bundled dataviz skill to advise printing y-axis tick labels in full under 10,000, and horizontal ones in full under a million where they fit
  • Updated the bundled dataviz skill to answer donut and pie chart requests with ranked bars or a segmented bar that prints its values
  • Changed Claude's file tools to ask before editing the local copy of your organization's server-managed settings, as they do for your settings files
  • Changed /ultrareview to check workspace trust before it runs git, as claude ultrareview does
  • Changed the Bash tool's shell to clear any inherited which alias or function and to stop passing exported which/unsetenv functions to commands, so which is the system command or zsh builtin
  • Changed /permissions Recently blocked to refuse approving a call you can't read in full, including one the terminal is too short to show
  • Changed auto mode in Cowork cloud sessions: a hook's allow of an MCP tool call now counts as no answer, so the classifier or a permission prompt decides
  • Changed hook if conditions such as Monitor(tail *) to match the Monitor tool's shell commands as Bash(tail *) matches Bash's
  • Changed the claude-api skill to ask to read a Managed Agents workflow run's workflow before changing the agent to improve that run
  • Changed flagged requests to retry on another model, not end in a refusal, when ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL, availableModels or deniedModels leaves only an older Opus model, or none
  • Changed idle compaction to also run for subscribers with telemetry turned off, and on Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and LLM gateways once the one-hour prompt cache is on
  • Changed FORCE_HYPERLINK=false (also no and off) to turn hyperlinks off instead of on
  • macOS: Changed git grep in most commands that Claude runs to use the C locale, to avoid a reported memory leak in macOS's regex library on files that aren't valid UTF-8
  • [VSCode] Fixed "Clear authentication" for MCP servers reporting success when the saved sign-in could not be removed
  • [VSCode] Fixed missing spinner and Stop button while a queued message's hooks run
  • [VSCode] Fixed session group changes that cannot be saved, such as a delete, failing silently; an error notification now appears
  • [VSCode] Fixed Cmd+F / Ctrl+F not opening the find widget in the plan preview tab
  • [VSCode] Fixed the voice dictation shortcut (Ctrl+D) doing nothing under non-Latin keyboard layouts such as Russian, Greek or Hebrew
  • [VSCode] Fixed missed one-time saved scheduled tasks being deleted without asking when the extension opened without a chat
  • [VSCode] Changed CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_CFC_PROMPT to also stop the extension adding the Claude in Chrome instructions to a session's messages; the browser tools stay available
  • [Cloud sessions] Added an Include completed button to the Scheduled tasks page when finished one-off tasks are the only ones hidden, so you can show them without opening the Sort menu
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed recently used self-hosted environments never appearing among the recent environments on the new session card
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed cloud sessions reporting uncommitted changes every turn after Claude moved a branch to a commit it had pushed from another worktree
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the self-hosted environment details dialog in admin settings squeezing its content out of view in very short windows or at high zoom; the dialog now scrolls
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the permission mode picker staying on Auto after a running cloud or Remote Control session refused the switch; it now shows the mode in use and tells you
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved scheduled tasks: runs in Anthropic's cloud now load the plugins enabled on your claude.ai account
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved Test connection for GitHub Enterprise in admin settings to also connect the way cloud sessions do, and to warn you when that second test fails
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved cloud session transcripts: a rename row now names the new title, and repository and environment lists show as a table instead of one line of JSON
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed cloud sessions from the web, desktop and mobile apps to start even when a setup script exits with an error, instead of failing to start
  • [Remote Control] Fixed the permission mode button in Remote Control sessions showing the wrong mode until you typed; while your computer is online it now shows the real mode on open
  • [Claude Tag] Added a dismissible link to the Claude Tag API docs on the Bundles and Channels tabs in admin settings, for Enterprise organizations with Slack connected
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed @Claude !restart giving up after one failed workspace check in channels shared across Enterprise Grid workspaces; it now retries, then asks you to run it again
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed a second confirmation DM and channel note when you connect your Claude account from Slack twice from the same link within a few minutes
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed follow-up messages in Slack showing no sign of progress while Claude's session waits for a self-hosted runner; Claude now posts a wait notice in the thread
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude sometimes not answering a tag in its own thread in Slack Connect channels where both organizations have installed Claude
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Retry on plugin and skill pages in Claude Tag admin settings discarding unsaved access changes after a failed load; your edits now stay in place
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed the repositories control in Claude Tag admin settings showing the same action twice; its menu now lists only what the button doesn't already do

Added an optional groups list to Claude apps gateway upstreams: only developers in the listed IdP groups are sent to that upstream, on failover too
Added guardrail_trace to Claude apps gateway Bedrock upstreams, to log which Amazon Bedrock guardrail filter fired on a request, without the matched text
